q: Why is ROAS increasing while net profit is declining?

checks.what: tool: ROAS attempted or derived from its definition

answer:
Short answer — because your profit fell mainly from higher absolute ad spend, not from a weaker per-rupee efficiency. In other words: ROAS (a ratio) can improve while total ad investment rises enough to erase the margin gain.

Evidence (periods: 2026-10-06..2026-10-12 vs 2026-09-29..2026-10-05)
- Net profit: ₹-30,856 → ₹-82,963 (Measured)  
- Ad spend (P&L basis): ₹345,581 → ₹395,584 (Measured)  
  - Ad spend increase effect on Net profit: -₹50,004 (96% of the net-profit change) (Measured)  
- Contribution margin: ₹314,725 → ₹312,621; effect -₹2,104 (4% of the change) (Measured)  
- Platform note: the hit is concentrated on Meta (net profit position for meta moved from ₹-78,313 → ₹-139,244) (Measured)

What this means
- Measured: Net profit drop ≈ total ad spend increase (dominant, ~96% of the change).  
- Derived: If ROAS is rising, that only says each rupee of ad spend is earning more revenue on average — but if you spend many more rupees, total cost can still rise and crush profit.  
- Hypotheses to test (plausible, not yet proven): higher-volume but lower-margin campaigns were scaled; campaign mix shifted toward Meta where spend rose; product-level margins or taxes changed; increases in unallocated/inefficient spend (broad Advantage+ / specific adsets flagged by the diagnosis).

Caveat: I could not fetch the canonical net ROAS metric (net_roas is broken in the catalogue), so I couldn’t verify the ROAS increase directly — the above uses measured P&L lines and the diagnosis of the profit drop.

Next step suggestion: run platform- and campaign-level ROAS and ad_spend (Meta vs Google) and drill into the top campaigns/adsets driving the extra ₹50k spend. Want me to run that?
